Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we design an extensible software platform called `Epsilon` that can automate the integration of theoretical predictions by linking multiple tools and managing the flow of information between them. Within this structure, we develop a set of common tools that can be used by various research groups to facilitate the creation of new connectors for specific processes and the maintenance of existing ones. We demonstrate the effectiveness of `Epsilon` by successfully integrating a wide range of processes, including deep-inelastic scattering, hadron production, and flavor changing neutral current processes, and make the code available to the scientific community. 

In the second part of the paper, we outline the technical details of implementing the $n$-fold integration technique, which is a key component of evolution equations, and provide an overview of the various tools that can be used to compute it. We also discuss the performance characteristics of different tools and the overall efficiency of the overall integration process. 

The `Epsilon` framework, along with the precomputed evolution equations, can be accessed through a web interface or used as a standalone code, and is designed to be highly flexible and easily extendable to meet the needs of various research groups working on PDF fitting and phenomenological studies. 

We also present a detailed analysis of the accuracy of the compiled evolution equations and the impact of different tools on the overall integration process for a sample process, and provide guidelines for choosing the appropriate tools for specific use cases. 

The `Epsilon` framework is publicly available on GitHub, along with a sample connector for the DGLAP evolution equation, and can be used by the broader scientific community to develop new connectors for unimplemented processes and evolution equations. 

We anticipate that the `Epsilon` framework will play a crucial role in the development of future probability density functions that better capture the complexities of hadron structure and behavior.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Furthermore, we found that the exact algorithm and the Monte Carlo method produce significantly different p-value estimates for large sample sizes. This suggests that the Monte Carlo method may not be reliable in situations with large data sets. We've also developed an improved approximation of the paired-permutation test by combining our exact algorithm with the exact binomial distribution calculation. This improved approximation outperforms the standard implementation of the paired-permutation test under the normal approximation. Our code is available for use.

Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code and models of the system have been made available for download to facilitate future research.

However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. Furthermore, we outline the potential application in constructing certain modules whose lattice structure is known in advance, and provide advice on constructing modules with specific lattice properties.

We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, we have established that the Liouville theorem for harmonic functions can be obtained directly from the above-mentioned result, without the need to apply previous theorems concerning the dimensionality of the set of harmonic functions that grow at a subharmonic rate. Moreover, we have proven that the set of all harmonic forms that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional, which extends the applicability of the Harnack inequality to these specific types of manifolds. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.
